➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq. And this is one of the most important events in the AI market in years.

The company priced its shares at $83, putting its valuation at around $1.5 trillion. The IPO raised more than $81 billion, making it the largest in history. Another $26 billion was invested separately by Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, and other companies across the same AI ecosystem.

And the timing of this listing couldn't have been better.

The day before yesterday, Nvidia once again posted insane numbers. Quarterly revenue came in at $115.8 billion, twice as much as a year ago. Data centers alone accounted for $107.6 billion. In other words, money is still pouring into AI infrastructure at an enormous scale.

But Anthropic reveals the other side of this story. The company is growing rapidly, but at the same time, it has already taken on nearly $900 billion in future commitments for computing capacity. Essentially, Nvidia and other companies are generating hundreds of billions in revenue today because Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and others keep building more data centers and buying more computing power.

And this creates a rather interesting dynamic. Nvidia sells infrastructure to Anthropic. Anthropic spends enormous amounts of money on it. And now Nvidia is also helping finance Anthropic so it can keep growing and buying even more infrastructure.

This doesn't mean demand is artificial. Anthropic's revenue is growing at an incredible pace, and demand for AI is very real. But today, for the first time, the market gets a chance to publicly value one of the biggest buyers of all this infrastructure.

That's why I wouldn't focus only on the price at which ANT opens trading today.

If Anthropic surges after its listing, the market will get yet another confirmation that investors are still willing to fund AI at practically any price.

But if one of the most anticipated IPOs of the decade starts to struggle, the questions will quickly spread to the entire supply chain. Because Nvidia's seemingly endless revenue growth is only possible as long as someone is willing to keep paying for the construction of all this infrastructure.

Today, we'll finally see how much the public market is willing to pay for it.

🧠 Do you close winning trades early to feel safer?

Fear of losing unrealized profit can make you exit a trade too soon. If this becomes a habit, your average win may shrink to the size of your average loss, making consistent profitability more difficult.

Why does it happen? You may imagine blaming yourself if the gain disappears. Closing the position brings relief, but the urge to exit may be about escaping that discomfort rather than managing the trade.

Before your next trade, picture yourself choosing whether to hold or close. Ask whether fear of losing open profit is driving the decision. You can also practise by splitting a position in two: close one part and leave the other open. This may help you get used to holding winners gradually, though it cannot remove risk.
